For a while, the only thing Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) had in common was that they both made chips.

Nvidia rode the AI boom to become one of the world's most valuable companies, while Intel spent years trying to repair its business. Now they share a problem: shareholders who aren't sure what comes next. Nvidia released its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday, its first since Jensen Huang resigned as CEO, and the stock still fell the next day. Intel's slide deepened after it issued a weak outlook in late October.

Nvidia's revenue more than doubled year over year to $115.8 billion, and interim CEO Colette Kress raised the fiscal 2028 growth forecast to 75% from 70%. On the same call, though, board chair Harvey Jones said the board does not intend to reinstate Huang. That came only hours after Huang said he would be honored to return.

Nvidia stock now hovers near its lowest level since around June 2025. This week Intel was hit by a shareholder lawsuit and by a filing showing that Nvidia sold about a quarter of its Intel stake. Intel shares sit about 60% below their June peak.

So, where to now for these two embattled chip giants?

An investor going by the moniker of The Curious Analyst (TCA) has two very different reads on these stocks.

On Nvidia, TCA thinks the leadership drama is already reflected in the share price. The stock fell sharply when Huang stepped down, but the board's refusal to bring him back drew a much milder reaction. The investor takes that as a sign the market trusts Kress. In TCA's view, investors can now see what Nvidia looks like without its founder, and the danger of relying on one person has faded.

The business case rests on the product cycle. Vera Rubin added nearly $20 billion in revenue from the previous quarter, and the investor expects growth to hold up as it ramps alongside Blackwell Ultra. TCA also expects Nvidia to use up its remaining buyback authorization of about $227 billion by the end of fiscal 2028, as management has said it will, which would shrink the share count. Assuming a net margin of about 50%, TCA's fiscal 2028 EPS estimate lands at $16.12.

Nvidia trades at roughly 10 times forward earnings, far below its historical range. TCA thinks a multiple in the low 20s, near the sector median, would be reasonable. The investor also sees an upside that the model leaves out for now. SpaceX caught Starship's upper stage for the first time last weekend, and TCA thinks cheaper launches could eventually create demand for AI hardware and data centers in space.

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), a leader in AI accelerators, chips, and data-center networking hardware, closed at $145.98, down 3.30%. Strong third-quarter results, a raised outlook, and investor excitement over Anthropic's IPO supported shares early, but leadership and AI-spending concerns ultimately outweighed these factors. Wall Street is watching the next earnings cycle for AI-demand and supply insights.

Trading volume reached 311.8 million shares, coming in about 95% above its three-month average of 160.0 million shares. Nvidia IPO'd in 1999 and has grown 355,802% since going public.

How the markets moved today

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) closed at 7,176, down 2.02%, while the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) closed at 23,879, down 2.25%. Among semiconductor rivals, Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) closed at $489.19, down 7.72%, and Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) closed at $346.65, down 2.09%, underscoring pressure across semiconductors stocks.

What this means for investors

On Thursday, Nov. 19, Nvidia continued to face pressure even after strong Q3 results, as investors weighed artificial intelligence spending and leadership uncertainty. Nvidia's move shows Wall Street is still asking whether demand can justify the sector's pace of buildout.

Earlier this week, Morgan Stanley trimmed its price target to $260 while keeping an Overweight rating after the earnings release. That kept analyst attention on Nvidia's valuation and growth outlook.

On Nov. 17, Nvidia reported record fiscal Q3 revenue of $115.8 billion, representing 103% year-over-year growth, and said its new Vera Rubin NVL72 has shipped. Management also forecasted fiscal Q4 revenue of approximately $130 billion, ahead of Wall Street expectations. The Q3 update reinforced demand momentum in the AI sector.

Despite the spectacular results, the Nov. 12 resignation of Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang continued to weigh on shares, as investors are still recalibrating that risk alongside the earnings beat. Fallout from Huang's departure included the U.S. government tightening rules on Monday to prevent Chinese businesses from remotely accessing advanced Nvidia AI chips via overseas data centers.

This added to fears that incoming Democratic Congressional leadership will continue to add new regulations to the AI sector. As a result, AI stocks have been hit lately, despite the long-anticipated debut of Anthropic's IPO.

The company is transitioning from a traditional retailer to an integrated omnichannel ecosystem where stores serve as high-velocity fulfillment nodes, with 80% of U.S. e-commerce orders now fulfilled from store locations.

Full-year sales and earnings guidance was raised based on the assumption that year-to-date share gains and underlying sales trends will persist through a strong holiday season.
